newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire denounces aid shipment for refugees in east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire denounces aid shipment for refugees in east.

text.p: Zaire's government has denounced a symbolic consignment of humanitarian aid sent to its troubled eastern region by the United Nations and independent aid groups as a violation of its territorial integrity.

At the same time, the international community was grappling with how to create an intervention force to ensure that extra assistance can reach more than a million sick and starving refugees displaced by fighting in the Zaire-Rwanda border area.

In Kinshasa, Boguo Makele, the Zairean government spokesman and Information Minister, told Reuters that his country had no objection to aid arriving in the Central African country via the capital Kinshasa and being distributed to displaced Zaireans.

But he denounced aid taken into the rebel-held refugee town of Goma from Rwanda. "This constitutes a violation of our territorial integrity," he said. "Aid for the (Rwanda) refugees should be distributed in Rwanda."
More than a million Hutus fled from Rwanda to Zaire in fear of reprisals in 1994 after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis and their sympathisers.

Spain and France were in the forefront of efforts to create an international intervention force for the region, but both made it clear that they would do so only within the framework of a U.N. multinational force.
South African President Nelson Mandela said he was also prepared to send troops to Central Africa as part of an international force to bring peace to eastern Zaire.
"In principle, I am prepared to contribute troops," Mandela said in a joint television interview with South Africa's state broadcaster and CNN on Monday.
Mandela said he would send a delegation to the Great Lakes region of Central Africa to gather information that would allow him to decide how big a unit to commit.
The United States on Monday denied it was blocking creation of an international force, but said it had still seen no coherent plan for assembling one.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking to reporters accompanying Secretary of State Warren Christopher to a conference in Cairo. said Washington recognised a force was needed "The United States is not trying to block that force," he said. "We are trying to help that force take shape."

France and Spain have been pushing for an immediate dispatch of a multinational force of about 5,000 to save lives after war between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi rebels dispersed about 1.2 miilion Rwandan and Burundi Hutus from refugee camps. Hundreds of thousands of Zairean vilagers were also uprooted.

The other major Western powers with the means have reacted coolly to the proposal. The United Nations Security Council on Friday night called for such a force but set no date for it, to the anger of the international humanitarian community.

The Tutsi-led government in Rwanda which supports the rebellion in Zaire opposes the use of French troops. It accuses France of sympathy for armed Hutus in the refugee camps who led a 1994 genocide of up to a million Rwandan Tutsis and their sympathisers and then fled with Hutu civilians.

Monday's consignment of aid, the first from a foreign source to reach eastern Zaire from Rwanda in more than a year, failed to reach any needy in the Goma area, let alone more than a million scattered refugees.
It arrived in convoys from the Rwandan town of Gisenyi and was taken to a sports stadium in the city.

"We were expecting food today. We saw very little, only medicine and a few biscuits. There was no rice, no fish, no meat," said Laurent Kabila, leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Officials expected the aid to stay in the stadium during the night and the aid workers would return to Goma on Tuesday. Aid workers pulled out of Goma as rebels closed in two weeks ago.
